_link.title: I can describe the capacity and duration of long-term memory

toLevel2.stem: What is the capacity of long-term memory?

options.text: Potentially unlimited
options.feedback: Correct. Long-term memory has a potentially unlimited capacity, meaning there is no known upper limit to the amount of information it can store.

options.text: Seven plus or minus two items
options.feedback: Incorrect. The capacity of seven plus or minus two items describes short-term memory, not long-term memory.

options.text: Three to four items
options.feedback: Incorrect. This does not accurately describe the capacity of long-term memory, which is potentially unlimited.

options.text: Limited to one hundred items
options.feedback: Incorrect. Long-term memory is not limited to a fixed number of items; its capacity is potentially unlimited.

toLevel2.stem: What is the duration of long-term memory?

options.text: Relatively permanent
options.feedback: Correct. Long-term memory has a relatively permanent duration, meaning information can theoretically be stored for a lifetime.

options.text: 0.2 to 4 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 0.2 to 4 seconds describes sensory memory, not long-term memory.

options.text: 18 to 20 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 18 to 20 seconds describes short-term memory without rehearsal, not long-term memory.

options.text: Exactly 24 hours
options.feedback: Incorrect. Long-term memory duration is not limited to 24 hours; it is relatively permanent and can last a lifetime.

toLevel2.stem: Long-term memory is central to which of the following aspects of human functioning?

options.text: Identity, skill, and knowledge
options.feedback: Correct. LTM holds everything we know and have experienced, making it central to identity, skill, and knowledge.

options.text: Brief sensory processing only
options.feedback: Incorrect. Brief sensory processing is a function of sensory memory, not long-term memory.

options.text: Temporary information holding only
options.feedback: Incorrect. Temporary information holding is a function of short-term memory; LTM provides relatively permanent storage.

options.text: Reflexive motor responses only
options.feedback: Incorrect. While LTM does support procedural skills, it is much broader, encompassing identity, knowledge, and all forms of learned information.

toLevel2.stem: Which statement about long-term memory retrieval is accurate?

options.text: Not all stored information can always be retrieved on demand
options.feedback: Correct. Although LTM has relatively permanent storage, not all information can always be accessed when needed; retrieval can sometimes fail.

options.text: All stored information is always perfectly retrievable at any time
options.feedback: Incorrect. While information may be stored in LTM, retrieval can sometimes fail, meaning not all information is always accessible.

options.text: Information in LTM is automatically deleted after one year
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has a relatively permanent duration; information is not automatically deleted after any set period.

options.text: Retrieval from LTM is always instantaneous with no possibility of delay
options.feedback: Incorrect. Retrieval from LTM can vary in speed and is not always instantaneous; sometimes information cannot be retrieved at all.

toLevel2.stem: A person recalling the name of their primary school teacher decades later demonstrates which feature of long-term memory?

options.text: Relatively permanent duration
options.feedback: Correct. Recalling information from decades ago demonstrates the relatively permanent duration of long-term memory.

options.text: Limited capacity of seven items
options.feedback: Incorrect. This example demonstrates duration, not capacity. The capacity of LTM is potentially unlimited, not seven items.

options.text: Brief duration of a few seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recalling information from decades ago demonstrates the opposite of brief duration; LTM has relatively permanent storage.

options.text: Automatic deletion after childhood
options.feedback: Incorrect. The fact that the memory persists decades later shows that LTM does not automatically delete information.

toLevel2.stem: Long-term memory has a potentially unlimited capacity.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. There is no known upper limit to the amount of information that can be stored in long-term memory.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Long-term memory does have a potentially unlimited capacity; there is no known fixed limit.

toLevel2.stem: Information stored in long-term memory can theoretically be retained for a lifetime.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. LTM has a relatively permanent duration, meaning information can theoretically be stored for an entire lifetime.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Long-term memory does have a relatively permanent duration, and information can indeed be retained for a lifetime.

toLevel2.stem: Long-term memory has a potentially {{blank:1}} capacity and a relatively {{blank:2}} duration.
LTM holds everything we know and have experienced, making it central to {{blank:1}}, skill, and {{blank:2}}.
Although LTM has relatively permanent storage, not all stored information can always be {{blank:1}} on demand.

toLevel3.stem: Why is the capacity of long-term memory described as 'potentially' unlimited rather than simply 'unlimited'?

options.text: Because it is practically impossible to test an absolute upper limit, so the term reflects what is currently known from research
options.feedback: Correct. Since no research has found an upper limit to LTM capacity, the term 'potentially unlimited' reflects the evidence-based understanding while acknowledging that an absolute claim cannot be fully verified.

options.text: Because long-term memory has been shown to have a strict maximum capacity in laboratory research
options.feedback: Incorrect. No research has established a strict maximum capacity for LTM; the term 'potentially unlimited' reflects the absence of any known upper limit.

options.text: Because long-term memory capacity varies from exactly zero to exactly one thousand items
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM capacity is not measured in fixed item counts; the evidence suggests no known upper limit.

options.text: Because only short-term memory has an unlimited capacity, not long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Short-term memory has a limited capacity (approximately 7±2 items); it is long-term memory that has a potentially unlimited capacity.

toLevel3.stem: Why is the duration of long-term memory described as 'relatively permanent' rather than 'absolutely permanent'?

options.text: Because while information can last a lifetime, retrieval failures mean some stored information may not always be accessible
options.feedback: Correct. The qualifier 'relatively' acknowledges that although LTM storage can last a lifetime, not all information is always retrievable, and some may appear to be lost even if it is still stored.

options.text: Because all information in LTM is automatically erased after exactly ten years of storage
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM does not automatically erase information after any set period; the 'relatively' qualifier relates to retrieval accessibility, not automatic deletion.

options.text: Because long-term memory lasts only a few seconds longer than short-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has a dramatically longer duration than STM; it can last a lifetime, not just a few seconds longer.

options.text: Because sensory memory is more permanent than long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory lasts only 0.2 to 4 seconds; long-term memory is far more permanent.

toLevel3.stem: How does the capacity and duration of LTM compare to short-term memory?

options.text: LTM has much greater capacity and duration than short-term memory
options.feedback: Correct. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity and relatively permanent duration, while STM has a limited capacity of about 7±2 items and a brief duration of approximately 18-20 seconds without rehearsal.

options.text: LTM and short-term memory have identical capacity and duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM has limited capacity (7±2 items) and brief duration (18-20 seconds), while LTM has potentially unlimited capacity and relatively permanent duration.

options.text: Short-term memory has greater capacity and duration than LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM far exceeds STM in both capacity and duration.

options.text: Both stores have limited capacity but LTM has shorter duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity and longer duration than STM, not shorter.

toLevel3.stem: A person knows they learned their primary school teacher's name but cannot recall it when asked. What does this illustrate about long-term memory?

options.text: That information may be stored in LTM but not always retrievable on demand
options.feedback: Correct. The person's sense that they once knew the name suggests it is stored in LTM, but a retrieval failure prevents access at that moment.

options.text: That the information was never encoded into LTM in the first place
options.feedback: Incorrect. The person's recognition that they once knew the name suggests it was encoded; the difficulty is in retrieval, not encoding.

options.text: That LTM has a very limited duration of only a few seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has a relatively permanent duration; the inability to recall is a retrieval issue, not a duration limitation.

options.text: That LTM has reached its maximum capacity and cannot store any more information
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity; the issue is retrieval failure, not capacity limitation.

toLevel3.stem: Why is long-term memory described as 'central to identity'?

options.text: Because LTM stores personal experiences, knowledge, and skills that define who a person is
options.feedback: Correct. Identity is built upon accumulated personal experiences (episodic), knowledge (semantic), and abilities (procedural), all stored in LTM.

options.text: Because LTM only stores a person's name and nothing else about their life
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM stores a vast range of information including experiences, knowledge, skills, and beliefs — all of which contribute to identity.

options.text: Because identity is determined by sensory memory, which feeds into LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. While sensory memory is the initial stage of processing, identity is shaped by the accumulated information stored in LTM, not sensory memory itself.

options.text: Because LTM creates a new identity every time new information is encoded
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM builds upon existing stored information to form a continuous identity; it does not create a new identity with each new encoding.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains the difference between storage and retrieval in long-term memory?

options.text: Storage refers to maintaining information in LTM, while retrieval refers to accessing that stored information when needed
options.feedback: Correct. Storage is the maintenance of encoded information in LTM over time, while retrieval is the process of accessing and bringing that information back into conscious awareness.

options.text: Storage and retrieval are the same process and cannot be distinguished from each other
options.feedback: Incorrect. Storage and retrieval are distinct processes; information can be stored but not always successfully retrieved.

options.text: Storage occurs in short-term memory while retrieval occurs only in sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both storage and retrieval occur within the LTM system; they are not distributed across different memory stores.

options.text: Retrieval always succeeds whenever information has been stored in LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Retrieval can fail even when information is stored, which is why not all LTM content is always accessible on demand.

toLevel3.stem: The fact that a person cannot recall a specific memory proves that it has been permanently erased from long-term memory.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Incorrect. Inability to recall information may reflect a retrieval failure rather than permanent erasure; the information may still be stored in LTM.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Retrieval failure does not necessarily mean the information has been erased; it may still be stored but inaccessible at that moment.

toLevel3.stem: LTM capacity is described as 'potentially' unlimited because no research has established an {{blank:1}} upper limit to what can be stored.
LTM duration is described as 'relatively' permanent because information can last a {{blank:1}} but is not always {{blank:2}} on demand.
Knowing you learned your teacher's name but being unable to recall it illustrates that information may be {{blank:1}} in LTM but not always {{blank:2}}.

toLevel4.stem: An elderly woman can recall vivid details about her childhood home, including the colour of the curtains and the smell of her mother's cooking, even though she last lived there 60 years ago. Which features of LTM does this demonstrate?

options.text: Both the potentially unlimited capacity (multiple sensory details) and relatively permanent duration (60 years) of LTM
options.feedback: Correct. The multiple sensory details demonstrate LTM's extensive capacity, while the 60-year retention demonstrates its relatively permanent duration.

options.text: The limited capacity of LTM, since she can only recall a few details from her childhood
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recalling colours, smells, and other sensory details demonstrates LTM's extensive capacity, not limited capacity.

options.text: The brief duration of sensory memory, since the details are from sensory experiences
options.feedback: Incorrect. While the original experiences involved sensory processing, the 60-year retention demonstrates LTM duration, not sensory memory duration.

options.text: The limited duration of short-term memory, since the memories are from a long time ago
options.feedback: Incorrect. The 60-year retention far exceeds short-term memory duration; this demonstrates LTM's relatively permanent storage.

toLevel4.stem: A student is studying for a VCE exam and worries that learning new information will 'push out' old information from her long-term memory. Based on knowledge of LTM capacity, what should she be told?

options.text: LTM has potentially unlimited capacity, so learning new information will not displace previously stored knowledge
options.feedback: Correct. Because LTM has no known upper limit, learning new information does not push out old information. Any difficulty recalling old information is a retrieval issue, not a capacity issue.

options.text: Her concern is valid because LTM can only hold a fixed number of items, and new learning replaces old memories
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity; new learning does not replace old memories due to capacity constraints.

options.text: She should stop studying to prevent new information from interfering with all of her existing memories
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM's potentially unlimited capacity means continued learning does not threaten existing stored information.

options.text: She should only study information she has already learned, since LTM cannot accommodate new content
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM continually accepts new information throughout life without displacing old content.

toLevel4.stem: During a reunion, a man recognises his childhood friend's face immediately but cannot recall their name. Later that evening, the name suddenly comes to him. How does this scenario illustrate LTM storage and retrieval?

options.text: The name was stored in LTM throughout, but a temporary retrieval failure prevented immediate access; the later recall confirms the information was not lost
options.feedback: Correct. The delayed recall demonstrates that the information was stored in LTM the entire time; the initial inability was a retrieval failure, not a storage failure.

options.text: The name was only stored in short-term memory and was re-encoded into LTM when it was recalled later
options.feedback: Incorrect. A childhood friend's name would be stored in LTM, not STM; the delayed recall reflects retrieval of existing LTM content.

options.text: The name was permanently erased from LTM and the man created a new memory of it later
options.feedback: Incorrect. The eventual recall of the correct name demonstrates it was stored in LTM throughout; it was not newly created.

options.text: LTM has reached its maximum capacity, which is why the name could not be retrieved immediately
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity; the delayed retrieval reflects an access issue, not a capacity limitation.

toLevel4.stem: A polyglot speaks seven languages fluently, having learned them over decades. What does this demonstrate about LTM capacity?

options.text: That LTM has potentially unlimited capacity, as it can store the vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation of multiple entire languages simultaneously
options.feedback: Correct. Storing seven complete languages demonstrates the vast capacity of LTM, as each language contains thousands of words, grammatical rules, and pronunciation patterns.

options.text: That LTM is limited to storing approximately seven items, matching the number of languages
options.feedback: Incorrect. Each language contains thousands of items (words, rules, sounds); the seven-item limit describes STM capacity, not LTM.

options.text: That the polyglot must have forgotten other information to make room for the seven languages
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity; learning new languages does not require forgetting other stored information.

options.text: That the polyglot stores each language in short-term memory rather than long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Fluent languages learned over decades are stored in LTM; STM could not hold this amount of information.

toLevel4.stem: A patient with Alzheimer's disease progressively loses access to previously stored memories. Does this contradict the claim that LTM duration is relatively permanent?

options.text: No, because the memory loss is due to neurological damage disrupting retrieval pathways, not a normal limitation of LTM duration
options.feedback: Correct. Alzheimer's disease involves progressive neurodegeneration that damages the brain structures needed for memory storage and retrieval. This is pathological, not a normal limitation of LTM duration.

options.text: Yes, because it proves that LTM duration is only a few years at most
options.feedback: Incorrect. Alzheimer's is a disease that damages brain structures; healthy LTM can maintain information for a lifetime.

options.text: Yes, because it shows that all stored LTM information is automatically deleted over time
options.feedback: Incorrect. The memory loss in Alzheimer's is caused by disease, not normal automatic deletion; healthy LTM has relatively permanent duration.

options.text: No, because Alzheimer's disease does not affect memory in any way
options.feedback: Incorrect. Alzheimer's disease significantly affects memory; the point is that this is due to pathological damage, not normal LTM limitations.

toLevel4.stem: A musician who learned a complex piano concerto 30 years ago sits down and plays it with only minor errors. What does this demonstrate about LTM?

options.text: That LTM can store complex procedural information with relatively permanent duration, even when not recently practised
options.feedback: Correct. The ability to play a complex piece after 30 years demonstrates LTM's capacity for complex information and its relatively permanent duration for well-encoded procedural skills.

options.text: That the concerto was stored in sensory memory, which preserved the auditory experience for 30 years
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory lasts only seconds; the concerto was stored as procedural LTM for 30 years.

options.text: That LTM can only store simple information and the minor errors prove it has limited capacity
options.feedback: Incorrect. A complex piano concerto demonstrates LTM's extensive capacity; minor errors after 30 years actually demonstrate remarkable retention.

options.text: That the musician re-learned the entire concerto in the moment through short-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Playing a complex concerto requires extensive procedural knowledge stored in LTM; STM could not support this level of performance.

toLevel4.stem: A teacher notices that a student can recall information studied three months ago when given a hint but cannot recall it without any cue. What does this suggest about the student's LTM?

options.text: The information is stored in LTM but requires a retrieval cue to be accessed; the storage is intact but unaided retrieval fails
options.feedback: Correct. The successful recall with a hint shows the information is stored; the failure without a cue demonstrates that retrieval can depend on appropriate cues, even when storage is intact.

options.text: The information was never encoded into LTM and the hint creates a new memory each time
options.feedback: Incorrect. The fact that a hint triggers accurate recall indicates the information was already stored in LTM.

options.text: LTM has exceeded its maximum capacity, preventing retrieval without external assistance
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity; the issue is retrieval cue dependency, not capacity limitation.

options.text: The student's LTM duration has expired after three months, erasing all stored information
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has relatively permanent duration; the successful cued recall proves the information persists beyond three months.

toLevel4.stem: The elderly woman's recall of multiple sensory details from 60 years ago demonstrates both LTM's potentially unlimited {{blank:1}} and relatively permanent {{blank:2}}.
A man who recognises a face but cannot recall the name until later demonstrates that information can be {{blank:1}} in LTM even when {{blank:2}} temporarily fails.
A polyglot who speaks seven languages fluently demonstrates that LTM can store {{blank:1}} amounts of complex information without reaching a known {{blank:2}} limit.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher argues that LTM capacity cannot truly be 'unlimited' because the brain has a finite number of neurons and synapses. Which analysis best addresses this argument?

options.text: The argument has theoretical merit, but the term 'potentially unlimited' reflects the practical finding that no research has identified an upper limit to LTM storage in functioning human brains
options.feedback: Correct. While the brain's physical structure is finite, the capacity for synaptic connections is so vast that no practical limit has been demonstrated, justifying the 'potentially unlimited' descriptor.

options.text: The argument is entirely invalid because the brain has infinite physical resources for storing memories
options.feedback: Incorrect. The brain does have finite physical resources; however, the complexity of neural networks means no practical capacity limit has been found.

options.text: The argument proves that LTM capacity is limited to exactly the number of neurons in the brain
options.feedback: Incorrect. Memory is stored through synaptic connections and patterns, not on a one-memory-per-neuron basis, making the relationship far more complex.

options.text: The argument is correct and LTM should be described as having extremely limited capacity
options.feedback: Incorrect. Despite finite neural resources, no practical limit to LTM capacity has been demonstrated; 'potentially unlimited' accurately reflects current evidence.

toLevel5.stem: Studies show that people can recognise thousands of previously seen photographs with high accuracy, even after only brief exposure. What does this finding reveal about LTM capacity?

options.text: It provides empirical evidence supporting the claim that LTM capacity is vast, as thousands of distinct visual memories can be stored from brief exposures
options.feedback: Correct. The ability to recognise thousands of photographs demonstrates that LTM can encode and store a remarkably large number of distinct memories, supporting the potentially unlimited capacity claim.

options.text: It proves that LTM can only store visual information and not any other type of content
options.feedback: Incorrect. While this study uses visual stimuli, LTM stores all types of information including verbal, procedural, and emotional content.

options.text: It shows that LTM has reached its maximum capacity because participants could not recognise every single photograph
options.feedback: Incorrect. Less-than-perfect recognition likely reflects encoding or retrieval limitations, not a capacity ceiling.

options.text: It demonstrates that photographs are stored in sensory memory rather than long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recognition after delays of days or weeks demonstrates LTM storage, not sensory memory, which lasts only seconds.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that because people forget things, LTM duration cannot be 'relatively permanent.' Which evaluation of this argument is most accurate?

options.text: The argument confuses retrieval failure with storage loss; information may remain stored in LTM even when it cannot be accessed
options.feedback: Correct. Forgetting often reflects retrieval failure rather than permanent loss of stored information. The 'relatively permanent' descriptor acknowledges both the potential for lifelong storage and the possibility of access difficulties.

options.text: The argument is entirely correct and LTM should be described as having very brief duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. People can recall information from decades ago, demonstrating that LTM duration is far from brief.

options.text: The argument is correct because all forgetting is caused by information being permanently deleted from LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Forgetting can result from retrieval failure, not just storage loss; information may still be stored but temporarily inaccessible.

options.text: The argument is irrelevant because no one ever forgets any information stored in LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. People do experience forgetting, but this is often a retrieval issue rather than evidence against relatively permanent storage.

toLevel5.stem: A critic states that the concept of 'potentially unlimited capacity' is unscientific because it cannot be directly tested. Which response best evaluates this criticism?

options.text: The criticism raises a valid point about testability, but the claim is supported by the consistent failure of research to find any upper limit, making it the best current description
options.feedback: Correct. While proving something is truly unlimited is logically challenging, the persistent absence of any demonstrated upper limit across extensive research makes 'potentially unlimited' the most accurate available description.

options.text: The criticism is entirely valid and the concept should be completely removed from all psychology textbooks
options.feedback: Incorrect. The concept reflects the best available evidence and serves an important descriptive function, even if absolute proof of unlimited capacity is not possible.

options.text: The criticism is entirely invalid because unlimited capacity has been definitively proven in laboratory conditions
options.feedback: Incorrect. Proving unlimited capacity is logically impossible; the claim is supported by the consistent absence of any upper limit in research.

options.text: The criticism proves that LTM capacity is exactly seven items, the same as short-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Extensive evidence shows LTM capacity far exceeds STM; the seven-item limit applies only to STM.

toLevel5.stem: Elderly individuals often retain detailed childhood memories but have difficulty forming new memories (as seen in some forms of dementia). How does this pattern relate to the concepts of LTM capacity and duration?

options.text: It demonstrates that LTM duration can be very long for well-encoded old memories, while encoding problems can prevent new information from entering LTM
options.feedback: Correct. The preserved childhood memories show LTM's relatively permanent duration, while difficulty forming new memories reflects encoding impairment (e.g., hippocampal damage), not a capacity or duration limitation of LTM itself.

options.text: It proves that LTM has a strict capacity limit that was reached during childhood
options.feedback: Incorrect. The difficulty with new memories in dementia is due to encoding impairment from brain damage, not because LTM capacity was reached.

options.text: It shows that all LTM information is permanently lost after age 65
options.feedback: Incorrect. The retention of childhood memories directly contradicts this claim; the issue is with new encoding, not loss of existing memories.

options.text: It demonstrates that LTM duration is exactly as long as childhood and no longer
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM duration can span an entire lifetime; the difficulty with new memories is an encoding problem caused by neurological damage.

toLevel5.stem: A textbook states that 'everything you have ever experienced is stored permanently in LTM.' Which evaluation of this claim is most accurate?

options.text: The claim is an overstatement because not all experiences are encoded into LTM, and the 'relatively permanent' descriptor acknowledges that storage is not guaranteed to be absolutely permanent
options.feedback: Correct. Many experiences are never encoded into LTM (e.g., unattended sensory information), and the qualifier 'relatively' permanent acknowledges that some stored information may become inaccessible over time.

options.text: The claim is entirely accurate and supported by all available scientific evidence on human memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Not all experiences are encoded, and the claim overstates LTM's permanence; the correct descriptor is 'relatively permanent,' not 'absolutely permanent.'

options.text: The claim is accurate because sensory memory automatically transfers all information to LTM permanently
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only attended information from sensory memory enters STM, and only some STM content is encoded into LTM; the transfer is not automatic or complete.

options.text: The claim is correct because LTM has a limited capacity that ensures every experience is carefully preserved
options.feedback: Incorrect. LTM has potentially unlimited capacity, but this does not mean all experiences are encoded; encoding requires attention and processing.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher compares the memory systems of sensory, short-term, and long-term memory in terms of capacity and duration. Which pattern accurately describes the progression across these three stores?

options.text: Capacity: unlimited → limited → potentially unlimited; Duration: very brief → brief → relatively permanent
options.feedback: Correct. Sensory memory has unlimited capacity but very brief duration; STM has limited capacity and brief duration; LTM has potentially unlimited capacity and relatively permanent duration.

options.text: Capacity: limited → unlimited → limited; Duration: permanent → brief → very brief
options.feedback: Incorrect. This reverses and mischaracterises the capacity and duration progression across the three stores.

options.text: All three stores have identical capacity and duration with no meaningful differences
options.feedback: Incorrect. The three stores differ significantly in both capacity and duration, which is a key feature of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model.

options.text: Capacity: limited → limited → limited; Duration: permanent → permanent → permanent
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory and LTM have unlimited/potentially unlimited capacity, and the stores have very different durations.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that the distinction between 'potentially unlimited capacity' and 'relatively permanent duration' in LTM is confusing and unnecessary. Which evaluation best addresses this argument?

options.text: The distinction is important because capacity (how much can be stored) and duration (how long it is stored) are independent features that describe different aspects of LTM functioning
options.feedback: Correct. Capacity and duration address different questions: capacity asks how much LTM can hold, while duration asks how long stored information persists. Both are needed for a complete description of LTM.

options.text: The student is correct because capacity and duration are the same concept expressed in different words
options.feedback: Incorrect. Capacity (amount) and duration (time) are fundamentally different concepts; a store could have large capacity but brief duration, or vice versa.

options.text: The student is correct because LTM has neither capacity nor duration and both concepts are meaningless
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both capacity and duration are well-established, measurable features of memory stores that are central to the Atkinson-Shiffrin model.

options.text: The distinction is unnecessary because all memory stores have identical capacity and duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. Different memory stores have distinctly different capacities and durations, making the distinction essential for understanding the memory system.

toLevel5.stem: The argument that LTM capacity cannot be truly unlimited because the brain has finite neurons is theoretically valid, but the term 'potentially unlimited' reflects the practical finding that no {{blank:1}} has been identified.
The claim that 'everything is stored permanently in LTM' is an {{blank:1}} because not all experiences are {{blank:2}} into LTM in the first place.
